narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 58% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year grades had the strongest influence. Placing in the first decile (bottom 10%) of your class was much lower than the average of roughly sixth decile among accepted students, and this pulled the prediction strongly toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.9, while below the 3.23 average of accepted applicants, actually worked in your favor and pushed the prediction somewhat toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the other signals. Finally, your choice to attend part-time had a noticeable negative impact. Only 7% of accepted students planned to study part-time, and the model sees this choice as increasing the risk of not passing the bar.

Taken together, the low third-year class ranking and part-time status outweighed the modest benefit from your undergraduate GPA, leading the system to conclude you were more likely than not to fail the bar exam.

You should focus on improving your academic performance, consider studying full-time if possible, and retake the LSAT or strengthen other parts of your record before reapplying. Many students successfully improve these areas and gain admission in a later cycle. (218 words)
